item.title: U-Boot firmware flaws, EU CSAM scanning vote, and healthcare cyberattacks
Gitea CVE-2026-20896 exploitation, Injective npm compromise, and ShareFile shutdown warning
MODBEACON, XRING XQUIC, Zimbra XSS, and WP-SHELLSTORM Drive Threat Digest
Ill Bloom Crypto Wallet Drains and BlackCat Negotiator Sentencing
ShareFile, Gitea, U-Boot and Injective npm Threats Lead 24-Hour Security Digest
item.content:encoded:
Hackers exploit critical auth bypass in Gitea Docker image — Must Read

Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20896, a critical authentication bypass in default Gitea Docker images that lets unauthenticated attackers impersonate any user, including admins, by sending a trusted reverse-proxy header. Gitea users should upgrade to version 1.26.4 or restrict REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to trusted IPs and review logs for compromise.

  • Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20896, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in the official Docker image for the Gitea self-hosted Git service.
  • The flaw affects official Gitea Docker images up to and including version 1.26.2 in the default configuration, where reverse proxy authentication headers such as X-WEBAUTH-USER are enabled.
  • Because the official Docker image ships with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=* , Gitea can trust the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any source IP and allow an unauthenticated client to impersonate any user, including administrators.
  • Gitea released versions 1.26.3 and 1.26.4 to address CVE-2026-20896 and advised users to upgrade directly to the most recent release.
  • Singapore’s cybersecurity agency warned that CVE-2026-20896 is actively exploited and recommended restricting REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to specific trusted IP addresses if upgrading is not possible.

Police suspects Dutch hackers were involved in Odido breach — Must Read

Dutch police say they have strong indications that Dutch hackers were involved in Odido’s February breach, including a Dutch-language vishing call impersonating IT support before phishing led to data theft. The breach exposed personal data of millions of customers and was claimed by the ShinyHunters extortion gang.

  • The Dutch National Police said it found strong indications that Dutch hackers were involved in the February breach at telecommunications provider Odido.
  • Police said a Dutch-speaking man posed as an Odido IT employee in a phone call with Odido customer service shortly before the hack, after which phishing misled the company and data theft occurred.
  • Odido disclosed on February 12 that attackers accessed its customer contact system on February 7 and downloaded personal data affecting 6.2 million customers.
  • The exposed information may include names, addresses, mobile numbers, customer numbers, email addresses, IBANs, dates of birth, and some passport or driver’s license details, depending on the customer.
  • The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility for the breach and released an 88GB archive containing over 15 million records on its dark web leak site.

New MODBEACON RAT Uses gRPC Streaming for Encrypted C2 Traffic — Must Read

China-linked Silver Fox is using a new Rust-based RAT called MODBEACON, delivered through fake software installers and SEO poisoning, to target organizations in Asia. The malware uses encrypted gRPC streaming via Xray/V2Ray-style transport to maintain stealthy C2 communications and load plugins for further compromise.

  • QiAnXin attributed a new Rust-based remote access trojan called MODBEACON to the China-linked Silver Fox cybercrime group.
  • The mid-June 2026 campaign delivered MODBEACON through counterfeit software installers promoted via SEO poisoning and targeted technology, education, and state-owned enterprises.
  • MODBEACON is a memory-resident implant that can fetch additional modules, run operator commands, and maintain encrypted communications with attacker infrastructure.
  • QiAnXin said MODBEACON uses a separated loader and beacon, injectable configuration, a plugin-based architecture, and gRPC tunnel streaming reused from the Xray/V2Ray transport layer.
  • MODBEACON’s reported capabilities include host fingerprinting, in-memory plugin loading, heartbeat messages, command-result reporting, and scheduled-task persistence.

Zimbra urges customers to patch critical web client XSS flaw — Must Read

Zimbra is urging customers using the Classic Web Client to upgrade to ZCS 10.1.19 to fix a critical stored XSS flaw that can be triggered by malicious emails and expose session or mailbox data. The bug was reported by Google’s Threat Analysis Group, raising concern because Zimbra flaws have repeatedly been targeted by state-backed hackers.

  • Zimbra released Zimbra 10.1.19 to patch a critical stored cross-site scripting flaw affecting the Classic Web Client used to access the Zimbra Collaboration suite.
  • Attackers can exploit the flaw through specially crafted emails that execute malicious code when opened, potentially enabling theft of session data, account settings, or mailbox information.
  • Zimbra said the issue only impacts users of the Classic Web Client and urged those customers to upgrade to ZCS v10.1.19 as soon as possible.
  • The vulnerability has not yet received a CVE ID, and Zimbra has not said it is being exploited in the wild.
  • The flaw was reported by Google's Threat Analysis Group, and the article notes that Zimbra security issues have frequently been exploited by Russian state-sponsored hackers in recent years.

Hackers Use Fake Microsoft Entra Passkey Enrollment to Gain Microsoft 365 Access — Must Read

A threat actor tracked as O-UNC-066 is using vishing and a fake Microsoft Entra passkey enrollment flow to trick Microsoft 365 users into approving access and registering attacker-controlled passkeys on their accounts. The campaign abuses confusion around passkey adoption to enable account takeover and potential data extortion.

  • Okta is tracking a threat actor as O-UNC-066 that is targeting organizations across food and beverage, technology, healthcare, automotive, construction, and aviation with voice-based fake security requests.
  • The attackers register domains containing the word “passkey” and call targeted Microsoft 365 users to persuade them that they need to register a new Microsoft Entra passkey.
  • The phishing kit imitates the Microsoft passkey enrollment process while enabling the threat actor to register an attacker-controlled passkey against the victim’s Microsoft account.
  • The operator-controlled PHP phishing kit can adapt the victim’s experience in real time to different multi-factor authentication requirements, including SMS one-time passwords, time-based codes, and push notifications with number matching.
  • Okta said a threat actor linked to O-UNC-066 has operated a data leak site called Pink since April 2026, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracks the cluster as CL-CRI-1147 affiliated with The Com.

Attackers Exploit 'Ill Bloom' Vulnerability to Drain $3.1 Million From Cryptocurrency Wallets — Must Read

Coinspect says attackers exploited the “Ill Bloom” weak-randomness flaw in some older or lesser-known crypto wallets to drain about $3.1 million from 431 wallets, with more funds potentially exposed. Users should check public addresses at illbloom.org and, if matched, move funds to a brand-new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase.

  • Coinspect disclosed a crypto wallet flaw called Ill Bloom, where some wallet software generated recovery phrases with weak randomness that attackers could work out.
  • Coinspect confirmed a coordinated sweep on May 27 that drained about $3.1 million from 431 wallets, with roughly $2 million more moving from exposed wallets since then.
  • Coinspect says wallets created on hardware devices are not affected, and most mainstream software wallets are not affected, while the real risk is with older or lesser-known mobile wallets, some dating back to 2018.
  • The affected weak phrases can expose funds across every chain they control, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Rootstock, Tron, and Polygon addresses traced by Coinspect.
  • Coinspect advises users to check public wallet addresses at illbloom.org and, if there is a match, create a brand-new wallet with a brand-new recovery phrase and move funds there.

Injective Labs GitHub Compromise Pushes Wallet-Key-Stealing npm Packages — Should Read

Attackers compromised Injective Labs’ GitHub/npm release process to publish malicious @injectivelabs packages that stole crypto wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when used. Anyone who installed the affected 1.20.21 packages should upgrade to a clean version and treat any keys or seed phrases processed by them as compromised.

  • Unknown threat actors compromised the Injective Labs SDK project's GitHub repository and used it to publish the malicious npm package @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21.
  • The malicious version contained fake telemetry functionality that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when affected library functionality was used.
  • The threat actor also published version 1.20.21 across 17 additional @injectivelabs scoped packages that depended on and pinned the malicious SDK version, affecting potential transitive users.
  • The exfiltration mechanism queued multiple key derivations over a two-second window and sent them in an HTTPS POST request to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective[.]network.
  • Users who installed the malicious version are advised to update to the clean version 1.20.23, treat any private key or mnemonic phrase passed through the package as compromised, rotate them, and check for transitive dependencies.

Exposed Hacker Server Reveals WP-SHELLSTORM Backdooring Thousands of WordPress Sites — Should Read

Researchers found an exposed server belonging to the WP-SHELLSTORM crew, revealing automated campaigns that used known WordPress and Joomla plugin flaws to backdoor thousands of sites for resale. Site owners should urgently patch affected plugins, especially Breeze and Joomla JCE, and hunt for webshells and VShell-style impostor processes.

  • Researchers found an exposed server used by the WP-SHELLSTORM operation that contained about 800MB of files, including webshells, exploit scripts, scan results, command history, and command-and-control settings.
  • WP-SHELLSTORM targeted more than 1.4 million listed websites, but confirmed compromises were far fewer, with Ctrl-Alt-Intel counting 25,195 compromised sites and SOCRadar counting more than 5,700 active webshells.
  • The campaign mainly targeted WordPress sites with outdated plugins, and the Breeze caching plugin flaw CVE-2026-3844 produced the most reported backdoors, with more than 17,000 successful compromises claimed by the crew.
  • The exposed toolkit included 27 known flaws and used tools such as an obfuscated down.php webshell derived from BestShell, a SNOWLIGHT dropper, and the VShell backdoor.
  • SOCRadar also found evidence that the same crew previously targeted corporate Java systems through the Nacos flaw CVE-2021-29441 and obtained cloud keys, database passwords, and Alipay RSA private keys from 11 systems across nine companies.

URGENT - Progress Tells ShareFile Customers to Shut Down Storage Zone Controllers Over Security Threat — Should Read

Progress Software has told ShareFile customers to shut down self-hosted Storage Zone Controllers due to a credible external security threat, while cloud-only ShareFile accounts are not affected. The company has not disclosed the nature of the threat or when systems can safely come back online, so exposed controllers should be treated as possible incidents.

  • Progress Software told ShareFile customers to shut down Windows servers running Storage Zone Controllers in response to what it called a credible external security threat.
  • Progress temporarily disabled access to affected accounts and said it has no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile accounts or data.
  • Only Storage Zone Controller customers are affected, while standard cloud-only ShareFile accounts are not affected.
  • Progress has not disclosed what the threat is, who is behind it, or when customers can safely restart affected controllers.
  • The article advises customers to keep affected controllers offline, confirm they are running version 5.12.4 or later on the 5.x line or a 6.x release, and preserve logs while checking for unfamiliar .aspx files.

Six New U-Boot Flaws Could Let Malicious Images Crash Devices or Run Code at Boot — Should Read

Binarly found six U-Boot flaws in FIT image signature verification, including two that could allow code execution before a device verifies boot software. Vendors using U-Boot should pull the upstream patches now because no fixed stable release is available yet.

  • Binarly found six flaws in U-Boot, a bootloader used in devices such as home routers, smart cameras, and server management chips.
  • The flaws affect U-Boot’s handling of FIT images during signature verification and are reachable while U-Boot is still reading an untrusted image before checking the signature.
  • Two flaws, BRLY-2026-037 and BRLY-2026-038, could allow attacker-supplied code to run at boot because U-Boot uses unchecked values returned by fdt_get_name.
  • Four flaws, BRLY-2026-039, BRLY-2026-040, BRLY-2026-041, and BRLY-2026-042, can crash the bootloader through out-of-bounds reads, a null pointer dereference, or stack exhaustion.
  • U-Boot merged patches for the six flaws in June, but there is no stable release containing the fixes yet, so vendors and maintainers are advised to pull the upstream fixes now.

Unpatched XRING Flaw in XQUIC Lets Remote Clients Crash HTTP/3 Servers — Should Read

A newly disclosed unpatched flaw called XRING in Alibaba’s XQUIC HTTP/3 library lets unauthenticated remote clients crash affected servers using a small amount of valid QPACK traffic. Until a fix is released, operators should disable QPACK’s dynamic table or turn off HTTP/3 support.

  • FoxIO researcher Sébastien Féry disclosed an unpatched flaw called XRING in Alibaba’s XQUIC QUIC and HTTP/3 library on July 8.
  • The flaw allows an unauthenticated remote client to crash a server using about 260 bytes of valid QPACK traffic, without malformed packets or login credentials.
  • Every XQUIC release through v1.9.4 is affected, and there was no fixed release or CVE as of July 10.
  • The issue affects any server that embeds XQUIC and serves HTTP/3 with default QPACK settings, including Alibaba’s Tengine web server according to FoxIO.
  • Until a fix is available, operators can set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY to 0 to disable QPACK’s dynamic table or disable HTTP/3 support entirely.

Study of 281 Free Android VPN Apps Finds Traffic Leaks, Unencrypted Data, and Tracking — Should Read

A study of 281 popular free Android VPN apps found widespread security and privacy failures, including traffic leaks, plaintext data, weak encryption, tracking, and five apps that could let attackers hijack VPN tunnels. The takeaway is that many free VPN apps do not provide the privacy or security they advertise, even when distributed through Google Play.

  • Researchers tested 281 popular free Android VPN apps from the Google Play Store with a framework called MVPNalyzer and found that apps flagged with at least one problem had more than 2.4 billion installs.
  • The study found that 29 apps leaked user traffic outside the encrypted tunnel, including 24 that leaked DNS traffic and six that leaked full browsing traffic.
  • Five apps downloaded configuration files without encryption, allowing an attacker on the same network to rewrite the file and redirect the VPN connection to a server they controlled.
  • The researchers found that 76 apps sent the device’s Advertising ID and that 246 apps contacted known advertising and tracking servers.
  • In a separate review of OpenVPN configuration files from 108 apps, only one followed every security best practice measured by the study.

China, India ran separate spying campaigns against same Pakistani police force — Should Read

SentinelOne says China- and India-linked hackers ran separate espionage campaigns against Pakistan’s Balochistan Police for more than two years, in some cases compromising the same systems. The operations targeted sensitive law enforcement data, likely to monitor security threats tied to Chinese interests in Pakistan and the India-Pakistan rivalry.

  • SentinelOne reported that hacking groups linked to China and India conducted separate, unconnected espionage operations against the Balochistan Police in Pakistan between February 2024 and April 2026.
  • The compromised police systems held sensitive data including criminal records, biometric and fingerprint data, personnel files, hotel and tenant registrations linked to national identity records, and citizen complaints.
  • SentinelLabs assessed that the China-linked activity was primarily driven by Beijing’s interest in protecting Chinese nationals in Pakistan connected to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.
  • SentinelLabs said the India-linked activity was likely connected to the rivalry between India and Pakistan, including accusations related to the Baloch insurgency and Kashmir.
  • The report said a China-linked operator planted malware disguised as an update on the Balochistan Police Complaint Management System, exposing both police users and citizens who used the portal.

Former ransomware negotiator gets 4 years for BlackCat attacks — Should Read

Former DigitalMint ransomware negotiator Angelo Martino was sentenced to 70 months in prison for helping carry out BlackCat ransomware attacks against U.S. organizations and sharing victims’ confidential negotiation details to maximize extortion payments.

  • Former DigitalMint employee Angelo Martino was sentenced to 70 months in prison for targeting U.S. companies in BlackCat ransomware attacks.
  • Martino pleaded guilty to his role in the attacks along with former Sygnia and DigitalMint ransomware negotiators Kevin Tyler Martin and Ryan Clifford Goldberg.
  • Court documents said Martino was directly involved in BlackCat ransomware attacks with Goldberg and Martin between April 2023 and April 2025.
  • Prosecutors said Martino shared confidential information about victims' insurance policy limits and negotiation positions with BlackCat operators while working as a negotiator for five victims.
  • The victims included at least five U.S. organizations, including a financial services firm that paid $25,660,000 and a nonprofit that paid $26,793,000.

Researcher Details WhatsApp-to-Host Attack Chain Using Three OpenClaw Flaws — Should Read

Three now-patched OpenClaw flaws could let attackers trigger credential theft, privilege escalation, sandbox escape, and host code execution, reportedly even from an external WhatsApp message. Users should upgrade to OpenClaw 2026.6.6 and restrict risky tool access such as exec for untrusted or channel-facing agents.

  • Three now-patched high-severity flaws in the OpenClaw personal AI assistant could enable credential theft, privilege escalation, and arbitrary code execution on the host.
  • The vulnerabilities are tracked as GHSA-hjr6-g723-hmfm, GHSA-9969-8g9h-rxwm, and GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc, and all three were fixed in OpenClaw version 2026.6.6.
  • Security researcher Chinmohan Nayak said the flaws can be used to trigger host code execution from an external message sent via WhatsApp.
  • GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc involves a path traversal and link following issue that could allow sandbox bind mounts to bypass parent-directory denylist checks.
  • The article recommends upgrading OpenClaw, enabling sandbox mode for all non-main sessions, removing exec from the tool allowlist for channel-facing agents, and monitoring for git clone commands using the ext:: external protocol helper.

Europe revives law allowing big tech to scan for CSAM — Should Read

The European Parliament revived a legal exemption allowing major tech companies like Google, Microsoft and Meta to voluntarily scan users’ messages for child sexual abuse material until 2028. Critics say the procedural vote undermined privacy protections and foreshadows a larger fight over “Chat Control 2.0,” which could mandate scanning even in encrypted services.

  • The European Parliament voted to revive a 2021 rule allowing big tech companies to voluntarily scan users’ messages for child sexual abuse material.
  • The revived rule gives companies such as Google, Microsoft, and Meta legal cover to continue CSAM scanning until 2028.
  • The vote used an unusual procedure requiring an absolute majority to kill the provision, meaning absent lawmakers were effectively counted in favor of the measure.
  • Critics said the procedural move was disturbing because Parliament had rejected the same measure three months earlier under normal circumstances.
  • A larger dispute continues over a proposed permanent framework called Chat Control 2.0, which could force service providers to scan conversations and hosted content, including end-to-end encrypted communications.

Ryuk ransomware member pleads guilty in the US, faces 15 years in prison — Should Read

Karen Serobovich Vardanyan, an Armenian man accused of helping deploy Ryuk ransomware against U.S. organizations, has pleaded guilty after extradition and faces up to 15 years in prison. Prosecutors say the group received about 1,610 BTC in ransom payments, while Vardanyan agreed to pay more than $1.1 million in restitution.

  • Karen Serobovich Vardanyan, a 34-year-old Armenian man, pleaded guilty to hacking U.S. companies and deploying Ryuk ransomware to encrypt their systems.
  • Vardanyan was arrested in Kyiv in April 2025, extradited to the United States, and had been indicted by a federal grand jury in Portland in February 2024.
  • Court documents say Vardanyan helped deploy Ryuk ransomware on multiple U.S. organizations between November 2019 and April 2020 after illegally accessing their systems.
  • The U.S. Department of Justice said Vardanyan and his co-conspirators received about 1,610 bitcoins in ransom payments, valued at around $15 million at the time.
  • Vardanyan is scheduled to be sentenced in September 2026 and faces a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison, fines of $250,000 for each of two charges, and more than $1.1 million in restitution.

License plate cameras may be next target after Supreme Court reins in location tracking — Should Read

A recent Supreme Court ruling requiring warrants for cell phone geofence searches could strengthen legal challenges against police use of automated license plate reader databases. Experts say the decision may reshape how law enforcement can access large-scale retrospective location data, though ALPR vendor Flock Safety argues the ruling does not apply to license plate cameras.

  • The Supreme Court’s Chatrie v. United States ruling found that searches of cell phone location history require a warrant and could affect the use of automated license plate readers.
  • Flock Safety says it has between 90,000 and 100,000 license plate reader cameras on public roadways and collects data on about 20 billion license plates each month.
  • Michael Soyfer of the Institute for Justice said the ruling emphasized the retrospective and indiscriminate nature of location surveillance, which he said also applies to automated license plate reader data.
  • Flock Safety said the Supreme Court decision is not relevant to its technology because Google location history comes from a person’s mobile device while its license plate readers capture point-in-time images of vehicles in public view.
  • Andrew Guthrie Ferguson said modern license plate readers connect to larger police and public databases that can contain social media activity, surveillance video, body camera footage, drone footage, gunshot sensor data, and dashboard camera footage.

The Email With Nothing to Scan: A 1 MB HTML Attachment That Renders Its Own Phishing Page — Should Read

A phishing email from an authenticated first-time Gmail sender used a large self-contained HTML attachment that rendered the credential-harvesting page locally, leaving no URL for gateways to reputation-check and exceeding deep inspection limits. The key defense is behavioral and post-delivery detection, not relying on SPF/DKIM/DMARC or static scanning alone.

  • An external first-time Gmail sender delivered a one-line email with a 1 MB HTML attachment named like a full report.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC all passed because the message was genuinely sent through Gmail and signed by a gmail.com key.
  • The HTML attachment rendered its phishing page locally in the browser, so no malicious URL appeared in the message for a Secure Email Gateway to reputation-check.
  • The static scan returned a clean verdict, and deeper content-level inspection failed because the file exceeded the analyzer’s processing limit.
  • The article says the useful detection signals were behavioral indicators such as a first-time external sender, no prior correspondence, a high-risk flag, and a one-line body pushing a large attachment.

Laser Attack Resets Tangem Wallet Passwords on Cards That Can't Be Patched — May Read

Ledger Donjon researchers showed that a costly, invasive laser fault-injection attack can reset passwords on Tangem wallet cards without the old password or backup card, potentially letting someone with physical possession move funds. The risk is low for most users because it requires a specialized lab and visibly destroys the card, but lost or stolen cards holding significant value should be treated as unsafe.

  • Ledger's Donjon security team demonstrated that a precisely timed laser pulse aimed at the chip inside a Tangem crypto wallet card can reset the card's password to an attacker-chosen value.
  • The attack requires physical possession of the card, cutting it open to expose the chip, specialized equipment estimated at about $250,000, and cannot be performed over the internet.
  • Tangem cards cannot receive firmware updates, so cards already sold cannot be patched against this flaw.
  • Tangem said the method is a lab-only physical attack, noted that Donjon belongs to rival Ledger, and argued that the practical risk for everyday users is virtually non-existent.
  • The article advises users whose Tangem card is lost or stolen and holds serious value to move their funds using another card in the set or a seed phrase if available.

Money launderer accused of stealing seized crypto while in prison — May Read

Bulgarian money launderer Rossen Iossifov has been charged with allegedly stealing and laundering $290,000 in government-seized cryptocurrency while already serving a federal prison sentence. Prosecutors say the funds were tied to his earlier role laundering millions for an online auction fraud network that victimized Americans.

  • Bulgarian national Rossen G. Iossifov has been charged in the Eastern District of Kentucky with stealing $290,000 in government-seized cryptocurrency while serving a 121-month prison sentence.
  • Prosecutors allege that in January 2024 Iossifov conspired with others to move the cryptocurrency from a seized account through multiple crypto exchanges and mixing services to keep it from the government.
  • Iossifov’s earlier conviction stemmed from his ownership and operation of RG Coins, a cryptocurrency exchange in Sofia, Bulgaria, used by Romanian members of the Alexandria Online Auction Fraud Network.
  • The fraud network posted fake Craigslist and eBay ads for high-value goods, typically vehicles, and victimized at least 900 Americans before converting payments into cryptocurrency.
  • Court documents say Iossifov collected more than $184,000 after laundering nearly $5 million for four network members, and he faces up to 25 years in prison if convicted of the new charges.

Cybercriminals Flock to Healthcare Businesses as Attacks Surge — Optional

Healthcare cyberattacks are rising fastest against service providers and other healthcare businesses, more than doubling in early 2026, while hospitals continue to face social engineering, impersonation, legacy device, staffing, and third-party risk challenges.

  • Cyberattacks against hospitals and clinics grew modestly in the first half of 2026.
  • Attacks on service providers and other healthcare businesses more than doubled in the first half of 2026.
  • Hospitals are seeing more impersonation and social engineering-driven attacks, according to Health-ISAC chief security officer Errol Weiss.
  • Errol Weiss said hospital CISOs are taking these threats seriously but face resource challenges in protecting hospital networks.
  • Errol Weiss cited legacy medical device complexity, always-on clinical operations, and heavy third-party dependence as structural realities that give attackers opportunities.

One admin equals one risk: Why cyber protection needs role-based control — Optional

Acronis Cyber Protect Cloud includes built-in roles for least-privilege access, but only about 4.8% of active customer tenants use any fitted specialty role, leaving most organizations over-reliant on default admin privileges. The key recommendation is for customers and MSPs to narrow access now by assigning role-based permissions such as cyber administrator, protection administrator, read-only, restore operator, or security analyst instead of broad administrator rights.

  • Across all active Acronis Cyber Protect Cloud customer tenants, only about 4.8% have granted at least one fitted specialty role alongside the defaults, while roughly 95.2% have granted none.
  • About 33.9% of customer tenants have no local administrator account because they are administered entirely from the managing partner level.
  • The most adopted fitted customer role is Administrator (protection) at about 2.41% of customer tenants, followed by File Sync and Share user at 1.11%, File Sync and Share administrator at 0.94%, read-only administrator (protection) at 0.77%, cyber administrator at 0.58%, and security analyst at 0.10%.
  • About 3.35% of partner tenants have granted at least one Partner Portal role, and Partner Portal Administrator is the most adopted partner role at 2%.
  • The article recommends that SMBs, MSPs, and customers working with MSPs reduce routine use of default administrator roles and use fitted roles such as cyber administrator, administrator (protection), read-only administrator (protection), restore operator, and security analyst.

The Replicant in Your Directory: AI Agents and the Identity Security Gap — Optional

AI agents and other machine identities are rapidly expanding enterprise identity risk because they often lack clear ownership, lifecycle controls, and visibility. The key takeaway is that organizations must continuously track what non-human identities exist, what they can access, who owns them, and when they should be retired.

  • Machine identities such as AI agents, service accounts, OAuth applications, and workload identities already outnumber people in many enterprise environments and can remain active after the applications or automation that created them are forgotten.
  • The article says identity security programs were built around human lifecycle events, while AI agents and other machine identities can be created automatically, inherit permissions, interact across systems, and create additional identities.
  • In 2025, threat actor UNC6395 obtained an OAuth token associated with Salesloft's Drift chat integration and used it to move through Salesforce environments across hundreds of organizations.
  • Netwrix's 2026 Data and Identity Security Report found that organizations where AI significantly expanded the number of identities reported a 43% breach rate over the previous year, compared with 11% where AI had not significantly changed the identity footprint.
  • The article argues security teams need continuous answers about what identities exist, who owns them, what they can access, and when they should no longer exist.

From 17,000 to 1.1 Million Assets: How Lumen Technologies Rebuilt Exposure Management at Scale — Optional

Lumen Technologies used Axonius to consolidate data from 40+ systems and discovered its asset inventory was vastly understated, growing from about 17,000 known assets to 1.1 million devices. The key takeaway is that trusted asset visibility is foundational to effective exposure management, faster zero-day response, and risk-based remediation.

  • Lumen Technologies used Axonius to reconcile data from more than 40 disconnected IT and security systems into one trusted asset view.
  • Lumen’s known cyber assets increased from about 17,000 across existing inventories to 500,000 after initial reconciliation and approximately 1.1 million devices currently.
  • With Axonius, Lumen can identify systems affected by a critical vulnerability, determine whether they are externally exposed, and establish ownership within minutes.
  • Lumen built an Application Posture Dashboard in Axonius by correlating CMDB relationships with control coverage, vulnerability data, and end-of-life status.
  • Lumen said Axonius visibility into end-of-life systems contributed to a decision to migrate most infrastructure to the cloud, reducing overall risk by 40%.

NIST Elevated DNS Security. Censys Active DNS Connects Names to Live Internet Infrastructure. — Optional

Censys is promoting Active DNS as a way to connect domain names to live internet infrastructure, DNS history, exposed services, certificates, vulnerabilities, and threat context. The key takeaway is that DNS visibility is increasingly positioned as evidence for exposure management and incident response under NIST CSF 2.0 alignment.

  • NIST SP 800-81r3 is mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, giving DNS security a clearer place in a framework used for risk, governance, and security operations.
  • Censys Active DNS actively resolves domain names by querying authoritative infrastructure and connects those results to the broader Censys Internet Map.
  • Censys Active DNS provides current and historical DNS records across A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SOA, and TXT records, including when records were first and last observed by Censys.
  • Security teams can pivot from a domain to resolved hosts, open ports, running services, TLS certificates, HTTP content, vulnerabilities, screenshots, host reputation, and Censys threat context.
  • The article says Censys Active DNS can support exposure management, threat hunting, detection engineering, incident response, and SOC triage for teams aligning to CSF 2.0.

item.title: OpenMandriva Alleges Contributor Sabotage After Repository Deletions and Package Obsoletions
Injective SDK, Braintree.Net Supply Chain Malware, GigaWiper, and UAT-7810 ORBs
